The True big-scale tetra, Brycinus macrolepidotus, is a substantial characiform from West and Central African rivers, attaining maximum dimensions that are notable among its congeners. Field surveys indicate the species reaches a maximum recorded total length of 53 centimeters [Li = 53 centimeters], a size that positions it as one of the larger members of the Alestidae family in its region. Larger-bodied individuals are typically gravid females, suggesting that substantial somatic growth continues well beyond the onset of reproductive activity. In terms of body mass and developmental milestones, the transition from larval to juvenile stages is marked by a surprisingly modest birth size. At a controlled water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the wet weight at birth is only 0.00069 grams [Wwb = 0.00069 grams], a minuscule starting mass that is consistent with the production of small, planktonic eggs typical of many open-water spawning characids. This initial wet weight contrasts sharply with the considerable size the species can achieve over its lifetime.

Juvenile growth in Brycinus macrolepidotus is rapid, and the onset of gonadal development occurs once individuals reach a distinct morphological benchmark. Detailed length-frequency analyses from several riverine populations show that sexual maturity is attained at a total length of 18.5 centimeters [Lp = 18.5 centimeters]. Puberty at this size allows the fish to begin participating in spawning aggregations while still well below their asymptotic length, a common strategy among iteroparous freshwater teleosts. The period between hatching and the commencement of exogenous feeding is brief under optimal thermal conditions. At a water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the age at birth, corresponding to the moment of hatching from the chorion, is approximately 4.5 days [ab = approximately 4.5 days]. This rapid developmental rate reflects the energetic advantages of warm, stable tropical waters, which accelerate enzymatic processes during embryogenesis and minimize the duration of the vulnerable yolk-sac stage.

Reproductive output in this species is substantial, driven by high fecundity per spawning event. At a stable water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], adult females at a body mass of approximately 1.7 kilograms produce around 58 eggs per day [Ri = around 58 eggs per day], a rate that accumulates into a significant annual fecundity over the protracted spawning season. This figure, derived from comparative fecundity estimates for the related pike characid Hepsetus odoe, highlights the capacity of B. macrolepidotus for rapid population turnover in productive floodplain environments. The ultimate wet weight of the species, representing the maximum published body mass for adults, is 2000 grams [Wwi = 2000 grams]. Reaching this upper mass requires several years of successful foraging, and not all individuals in a cohort will attain this size due to ecological constraints such as food limitation and predation pressure during the juvenile phase.

Longevity estimates for Brycinus macrolepidotus suggest a relatively extended life span for a tropical characiform, which is consistent with its large body size and moderate metabolic demands. Under natural thermal regimes averaging 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum documented life span is approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years], allowing for multiple reproductive seasons. Individuals that survive the high early mortality associated with the planktonic larval phase can contribute to spawning aggregations over several consecutive years. The slow pace of senescence in this species is ecologically adaptive, providing a buffer against years of poor recruitment by enabling older, reproductively experienced females to dominate the annual egg output. In captivity, where predation is removed and food is consistent, individuals may occasionally exceed this lifespan, but the wild record solidly supports the 7-year figure as a reliable benchmark for this species (7 years) [am = 7 years] at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C].

The spatial ecology and trophic position of the true big-scale tetra are closely linked to its life history traits. As a pelagic predator in open river channels and floodplain lakes, it preys heavily on smaller fish and large zooplankton, a diet that fuels its attainment of a 2000-gram body mass (2000 grams) [Wwi = 2000 grams]. In comparison to congeners such as Brycinus longipinnis, which matures at a smaller size, B. macrolepidotus delays maturity, reaching a total length of 18.5 centimeters [Lp = 18.5 centimeters] before the first spawning event. This strategy results in a higher lifetime fecundity, as larger females carry more gonadal tissue. The species is also sensitive to temperature; the hatching window at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] remains a tight 4.5 days [ab = 4.5 days], and deviations outside this thermal optimum lengthen the yolk-sac period. The maximum recorded total length of 53 centimeters [Li = 53 centimeters] is occasionally rivaled by very old females, but such individuals are rare in heavily fished populations.
